claim: Metformin is the first line therapy for type 2 diabetes and the most frequently prescribed oral hypoglycemic medication worldwide.
source: Metformin is the first line therapy for type 2 diabetes and the most frequently prescribed oral hypoglycemic medication worldwide (Inzucchi et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Inzucchi et al., 2012

claim: Human epidemiologic studies note an association between metformin use and decreased incidence of cancer.
source: Human epidemiologic studies note an association between metformin use and decreased incidence of cancer (Evans et al., 2005; Yuan et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Evans et al., 2005 and Yuan et al., 2013

claim: Metformin extends lifespan in invertebrate and vertebrate models.
source: In addition, metformin extends lifespan in invertebrate and vertebrate models (Cabreiro et al., 2013; Martin-Montalvo et al., 2013; Onken and Driscoll, 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to Cabreiro et al., 2013; Martin-Montalvo et al., 2013; Onken and Driscoll, 2010

claim: Metformin may reduce aging-related diseases in humans.
source: and therefore may reduce aging-related diseases in humans (Barzilai et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barzilai et al., 2016 and speculative language 'may reduce'

claim: A conserved signaling axis connecting mitochondria, the nuclear pore complex, and mTORC1 inhibition is required for metformin-mediated extension of lifespan in C. elegans and inhibition of growth in worms and human cancer cells.
source: Our previous work identified a conserved signaling axis connecting mitochondria, the nuclear pore complex, and mTORC1 inhibition that is required for metformin-mediated extension of lifespan in Caenorhabditis elegans and inhibition of growth in worms and human cancer cells (Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu et al., 2016

claim: AMPK is not necessary for metformin-induced growth inhibition in C. elegans but is required for the drug's pro-longevity effects.
source: The energy sensor AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) is not necessary for metformin-induced growth inhibition in C. elegans but is required for the drug's pro-longevity effects (Cabreiro et al., 2013; Onken and Driscoll, 2010; Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cabreiro et al., 2013; Onken and Driscoll, 2010; Chen et al., 2017

claim: The longevity-promoting transcription factor SKN-1/Nrf is required for biguanide-mediated lifespan extension.
source: Consistently, mechanistic studies indicate that the longevity-promoting transcription factor SKN-1/nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor (Nrf) is required for biguanide-mediated lifespan extension (Cabreiro et al., 2013; Onken and Driscoll, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cabreiro et al., 2013; Onken and Driscoll, 2010

claim: Ether lipids are involved in the maintenance of general membrane fluidity and in the formation of lipid rafts within microdomains.
source: Ether lipids are involved in the maintenance of general membrane fluidity and in the formation of lipid rafts within microdomains, which are important for promotion of membrane fusion and cellular signaling (Glaser and Gross, 1994; Komljenovic et al., 2009; Marrink and Mark, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Glaser and Gross, 1994; Komljenovic et al., 2009; Marrink and Mark, 2004

claim: Ether lipids have broad roles in the regulation of cell differentiation.
source: Ether lipids have broad roles in the regulation of cell differentiation (Davies et al., 2001; Facciotti et al., 2012; Rodemer et al., 2003; Teigler et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citations to Davies et al., 2001; Facciotti et al., 2012; Rodemer et al., 2003; Teigler et al., 2009

claim: Ether lipids have roles in cellular signaling.
source: Ether lipids have broad roles in the regulation of cell differentiation (Davies et al., 2001; Facciotti et al., 2012; Rodemer et al., 2003; Teigler et al., 2009), cellular signaling (Thukkani et al., 2002; Albert et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to Thukkani et al., 2002; Albert et al., 2003

claim: Ether lipids have roles in reduction of oxidative stress through their action as antioxidants.
source: and reduction of oxidative stress through their action as antioxidants (Morand et al., 1988; Zoeller et al., 1988; Reiss et al., 1997; Maeba et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Morand et al., 1988; Zoeller et al., 1988; Reiss et al., 1997; Maeba et al., 2002

claim: Humans deficient in ether lipid biogenesis suffer from rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata (RCDP), a rare genetic disorder resulting in skeletal and facial abnormalities, psychomotor retardation, and is uniformly fatal typically before patients reach their teenage years.
source: Humans deficient in ether lipid biogenesis suffer from rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata (RCDP), a rare genetic disorder, which results in skeletal and facial abnormalities, psychomotor retardation, and is uniformly fatal typically before patients reach their teenage years (White et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to White et al., 2003

claim: Current evidence linking alterations in ether lipid levels to aging and longevity in humans is strictly correlative.
source: Thus, current evidence linking alterations in ether lipid levels to aging and longevity in humans is strictly correlative (Gonzalez-Covarrubias et al., 2013; Pradas et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gonzalez-Covarrubias et al., 2013; Pradas et al., 2019

claim: Ether lipid precursors are first synthesized by enzymes associated with the membranes of peroxisomes.
source: Ether lipid precursors are first synthesized by enzymes associated with the membranes of peroxisomes (Ghosh and Hajra, 1986; Hardeman and van den Bosch, 1989; Singh et al., 1993.)
evidence: Supported by citations to Ghosh and Hajra, 1986; Hardeman and van den Bosch, 1989; Singh et al., 1993

claim: The main enzymes involved in ether lipid biosynthesis within the peroxisomal matrix are glyceronephosphate O-acyltransferase (GNPAT) and alkylglycerone phosphate synthase (AGPS).
source: The main enzymes involved in ether lipid biosynthesis within the peroxisomal matrix are glyceronephosphate O-acyltransferase (GNPAT) and alkylglycerone phosphate synthase (AGPS).
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of ether lipid biosynthesis pathway

claim: Fatty acyl-CoA reductase 1 (FAR1) supplies most of the fatty alcohols used to generate the ether linkage in the precursor, 1-O-alkyl-glycerol-3-phosphate.
source: Fatty acyl-CoA reductase 1 (FAR1) supplies most of the fatty alcohols used to generate the ether linkage in the precursor, 1-O-alkyl-glycerol-3-phosphate.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of ether lipid biosynthesis pathway

claim: The ether lipid precursor 1-O-alkyl-glycerol-3-phosphate is trafficked to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) for acyl chain remodeling to produce various ether lipid products.
source: This precursor is then trafficked to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) for acyl chain remodeling to produce various ether lipid products (Hua et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hua et al., 2017

claim: In C. elegans, loss-of-function mutations of acl-7/GNPAT, ads-1/AGPS, and fard-1/FAR1 result in an inability to produce ether-linked lipids.
source: In C. elegans, loss-of-function mutations of any of the three main enzymes involved in human ether lipid biosynthesis, acl-7/GNPAT, ads-1/AGPS, and fard-1/FAR1, result in an inability to produce ether-linked lipids, as in humans, and has been reported to shorten worm lifespan (Drechsler et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Drechsler et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2016

claim: Loss-of-function mutations of acl-7/GNPAT, ads-1/AGPS, and fard-1/FAR1 in C. elegans have been reported to shorten worm lifespan.
source: In C. elegans, loss-of-function mutations of any of the three main enzymes involved in human ether lipid biosynthesis, acl-7/GNPAT, ads-1/AGPS, and fard-1/FAR1, result in an inability to produce ether-linked lipids, as in humans, and has been reported to shorten worm lifespan (Drechsler et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Drechsler et al., 2016; Shi et al., 2016

claim: Worms and human cells deficient in ether lipids exhibit compensatory changes in phospholipid species, including increases in phosphatidylethanolamines and phosphatidylcholines containing saturated fatty acids.
source: Worms and human cells deficient in ether lipids exhibit compensatory changes in phospholipid species, including increases in phosphatidylethanolamines and phosphatidylcholines containing saturated fatty acids (Rodemer et al., 2003; Benjamin et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rodemer et al., 2003; Benjamin et al., 2013

claim: In contrast to humans, ether lipid deficient nematodes develop to adulthood at a normal rate.
source: However, in contrast to humans, ether lipid deficient nematodes develop to adulthood at a normal rate, providing an opportunity to determine the biological roles of ether lipids in aging and longevity without pleiotropies associated with developmental rate.
evidence: Supported by comparison to human phenotypes and observation in C. elegans

claim: The ether lipid biosynthetic machinery is necessary for lifespan extension stimulated by metformin or phenformin in C. elegans.
source: Here, we show that the ether lipid biosynthetic machinery is necessary for lifespan extension stimulated by metformin or the related biguanide phenformin in C. elegans.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Phenformin treatment drives increases in multiple phosphatidylethanolamine-containing ether lipids through direct biguanide action on C. elegans rather than on the bacterial food source.
source: Metabolomic analysis indicates that phenformin treatment drives increases in multiple phosphatidylethanolamine-containing ether lipids through direct biguanide action on C. elegans rather than on the bacterial food source.
evidence: Supported by metabolomic analysis data presented in the manuscript

claim: Requirement for the ether lipid biosynthetic genes extends to multiple genetic longevity paradigms, including defective mitochondrial electron transport function (isp-1), defective pharyngeal pumping/caloric restriction (eat-2), and compromises in mTOR complex 1 activation (raga-1).
source: Interestingly, requirement for the ether lipid biosynthetic genes extends to multiple genetic longevity paradigms, including defective mitochondrial electron transport function (isp-1), defective pharyngeal pumping/caloric restriction (eat-2), and compromises in mTOR complex 1 activation (raga-1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Overexpressing fard-1, the enzyme that produces fatty alcohols for ether lipid biogenesis in C. elegans, extends lifespan.
source: We show that overexpressing fard-1, the enzyme that produces fatty alcohols for ether lipid biogenesis in C. elegans, extends lifespan, supportive of the idea that alterations in the ether lipid landscape alone is sufficient to promote healthy aging.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Ether lipids promote longevity downstream of biguanide action through activation of metabolic stress defenses and somatic lipid redistribution driven by the transcription factor SKN-1/Nrf.
source: Mechanistically, ether lipids promote longevity downstream of biguanide action through activation of metabolic stress defenses and somatic lipid redistribution driven by the transcription factor SKN-1/Nrf.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: A prior screen of ~1000 metabolic genes for RNAi knockdowns that interfere with the growth-inhibitory properties of metformin in C. elegans yielded fard-1 and acl-7.
source: A prior screen of ~1000 metabolic genes for RNA interference (RNAi) knockdowns that interfere with the growth-inhibitory properties of a high, 160 mM dose of metformin in C. elegans (utilized to maximize the sensitivity and specificity of our assay to identify true epistatic candidates) (Wu et al., 2016), yielded fard-1 and acl-7, which are required for ether lipid biosynthesis.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu et al., 2016 and experimental data

claim: RNAi knockdown of fard-1 and acl-7 reveals significant resistance to biguanide-induced growth inhibition.
source: Confirming our screen results, granular, quantitative analysis following RNAi knockdown of fard-1 and acl-7 reveals significant resistance to biguanide-induced growth inhibition (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Biguanide effects on growth in C. elegans share significant overlap mechanistically with the machinery by which metformin extends lifespan in the worm.
source: Our lab has previously demonstrated that biguanide effects on growth in C. elegans share significant overlap mechanistically with the machinery by which metformin extends lifespan in the worm, thus suggesting that modulation of ether lipid biosynthesis may also be responsible for the lifespan-extending properties of the drug (Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu et al., 2016

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in fard-1, acl-7, or ads-1 significantly abrogate lifespan extension induced by lifespan-extending doses of metformin (50 mM) and phenformin (4.5 mM).
source: Indeed, loss-of-function mutations in any of three genes encoding enzymes required for ether lipid biosynthesis, fard-1, acl-7, or ads-1, significantly abrogate lifespan extension induced by lifespan-extending doses of metformin (50 mM) and the related biguanide phenformin (4.5 mM) (Figure 1B–G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B–G

claim: Loss-of-function of ads-1 and acl-7 may display a modest increase in lifespan with metformin administration but display a percentage median lifespan increase significantly reduced in comparison to wild-type controls.
source: Loss-of-function of ads-1 and acl-7 may display a modest increase in lifespan with metformin administration but display a percentage median lifespan increase significantly reduced in comparison to wild-type controls (Figure 1B–G, and throughout manuscript see Supplementary file 1 for all tabular survival statistics and biological replicates).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B–G and Supplementary file 1

claim: RNAi knockdowns of fard-1 and acl-7 in wild-type worms partially impair lifespan extension promoted by phenformin.
source: Confirming that these mutations confer resistance to metformin by compromising ether lipid synthetic capacity, RNAi knockdowns of fard-1 and acl-7 in wild-type worms also partially impair lifespan extension promoted by phenformin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C

claim: Lifespan analyses performed without the use of FUdR reveal similar abrogation of biguanide-mediated lifespan extension with inactivation of the ether lipid synthetic machinery.
source: This dependency is not confounded by chemical inhibition of reproduction, as lifespan analyses performed without the use of the thymidylate synthase inhibitor 5-fluoro-2′-deoxyuridine (FUdR) reveal similar abrogation of biguanide-mediated lifespan extension with inactivation of the ether lipid synthetic machinery (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–F; Van Raamsdonk and Hekimi, 2011).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–F and citation to Van Raamsdonk and Hekimi, 2011

claim: Phenformin is more readily absorbed without need for a specific transporter, unlike metformin.
source: Studies from this point forward are presented predominantly with phenformin because phenformin is more readily absorbed without need for a specific transporter, unlike metformin (Wu et al., 2016; Sogame et al., 2009; Segal et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Wu et al., 2016; Sogame et al., 2009; Segal et al., 2011

claim: Phenformin provides more consistent lifespan extension than metformin in C. elegans.
source: and our experience indicates more consistent lifespan extension with phenformin in C. elegans.
evidence: Based on the authors' experimental experience

claim: A deficiency in ether lipid synthesis does not significantly impact levels of biguanides in metformin- and phenformin-treated C. elegans.
source: Thus, a deficiency in ether lipid synthesis does not significantly impact levels of biguanides in metformin- and phenformin-treated C. elegans.
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS data presented in Figure 1H–I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E

claim: Phenformin abundance is quantitatively similar across wild-type and the three ether lipid mutant strains.
source: A comparison of normalized concentrations of phenformin across all four strains shows that phenformin abundance is quantitatively similar across wild-type and the three ether lipid mutant strains (Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D

claim: Metformin levels are similar in wild-type vs. ether lipid mutant animals.
source: Similar results were obtained when comparing levels of metformin in wild-type vs. ether lipid mutant animals (Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E

claim: fard-1 mutants show absence of 18-carbon containing fatty alcohol derivatives (dimethylacetals [DMAs]) and an accumulation of stearate (18:0) relative to wild-type controls by GC-MS.
source: We first recapitulated the observation that fard-1 mutants show absence of 18-carbon containing fatty alcohol derivatives (dimethylacetals [DMAs], which indicate alkenyl ether lipid or plasmalogen levels) and an accumulation of stearate (18:0) relative to wild-type controls by GC-MS (Figure 2A—B; Shi et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A–B and citation to Shi et al., 2016

claim: Phenformin-treated wild-type worms display a significant increase in 18:0 DMA versus vehicle, whereas no such increase is evident in drug-treated fard-1 worms.
source: Strikingly, phenformin-treated wild-type worms display a significant increase in 18:0 DMA versus vehicle, whereas no such increase is evident in drug-treated fard-1 worms (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Relative proportions of stearic acid (18:0) levels within the total fatty acid pool are significantly increased in fard-1 mutants treated with phenformin versus vehicle-treated fard-1 controls.
source: In addition, relative proportions of stearic acid (18:0) levels within the total fatty acid pool are significantly increased in fard-1 mutants treated with phenformin versus vehicle-treated fard-1 controls (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2D

claim: The relative proportion of stearic acid does not rise in phenformin-treated wild-type animals, suggesting that stearate is being utilized for ether lipid production.
source: In comparison, the relative proportion of stearic acid does not rise in phenformin-treated wild-type animals, suggesting that stearate is being utilized for ether lipid production.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2D and inference from the observation

claim: Phenformin-treated wild-type animals show a significant increase in the less abundant 16:0 DMA and 18:1 DMA species.
source: In alignment, an assessment of levels of additional alkenyl fatty alcohols in phenformin-treated, wild-type animals indicates a parallel, significant increase in the less abundant 16:0 DMA and 18:1 DMA species (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Phenformin treatment leads to an overall increase of alkenyl ether lipid levels in C. elegans.
source: We conclude that phenformin treatment leads to an overall increase of alkenyl ether lipid levels in C. elegans.
evidence: Supported by GC-MS data presented in Figure 2

claim: Phenformin treatment results in a significant increase in four ether lipids: PE(O-16:0/18:1), PE(O-18:0/18:3), PE(O-18:0/20:2), and PE(P-18:1/18:1).
source: This analysis indicates that phenformin treatment results in a significant increase in normalized abundance of four ether lipids, PE(O-16:0/18:1), PE(O-18:0/18:3), PE(O-18:0/20:2), and PE(P-18:1/18:1), even when corrected for multiple hypothesis testing.
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS data presented in Figure 2G

claim: Phosphatidylethanolamine ether lipid abundances were extremely low in fard-1, acl-7, and ads-1 mutants and unchanged by phenformin treatment, unlike in wild-type animals.
source: Finally, phosphatidylethanolamine ether lipid abundances were extremely low in fard-1, acl-7, and ads-1 mutants and unchanged by phenformin treatment, unlike in wild-type animals (Figure 2F and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—source data 1

claim: Exogenously expressed FARD-1 (fard-1 oe1) is expressed in the intestine and localizes near structures resembling lipid droplets.
source: Exogenously expressed FARD-1 (fard-1 oe1) is expressed in the intestine and localizes near structures resembling lipid droplets by Nomarski microscopy (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B

claim: FARD-1 does not possess a predicted PTS, in contrast to ACL-7 and ADS-1.
source: FARD-1 does not possess a predicted PTS, in contrast to ACL-7 and ADS-1.
evidence: Based on sequence analysis and established knowledge of peroxisomal targeting sequences

claim: At baseline, FARD-1::RFP fluorescence partially overlaps with peroxisomally targeted GFP.
source: At baseline, FARD-1::RFP fluorescence partially overlaps with peroxisomally targeted GFP (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C

claim: Treatment with phenformin does not change the amount of overlap between FARD-1::RFP and GFP::PTS1 relative to vehicle-treated controls.
source: Colocalization analysis indicates that treatment with phenformin does not change the amount of overlap between FARD-1::RFP and GFP::PTS1 relative to vehicle-treated controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by colocalization analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D

claim: FARD-1::RFP fluorescence directly surrounds some, but not all, BODIPY-positive lipid droplets in the worm intestine.
source: We found that FARD-1::RFP fluorescence directly surrounds some, but not all, BODIPY-positive lipid droplets in the worm intestine (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E

claim: Phenformin does not alter the number of lipid droplets that are surrounded by FARD-1 or its distribution around lipid droplets.
source: However, as with peroxisomes, phenformin does not alter the number of lipid droplets that are surrounded by FARD-1 or its distribution around lipid droplets (data not shown).
evidence: Based on experimental observation (data not shown)

claim: FARD-1::RFP localizes into web-like structures in the fard-1(oe3) reporter that may represent smooth ER versus another cellular tubular vesicular network.
source: Finally, FARD-1::RFP localizes into web-like structures in the fard-1(oe3) reporter that may represent smooth ER versus another cellular tubular vesicular network (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F), and this localization is also not altered by biguanide treatment.
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2F and speculation about identity

claim: mRNAs encoding FARD-1, ACL-7, and ADS-1 decreased or remain unchanged in abundance upon treatment with biguanide.
source: We next examined expression of mRNAs encoding FARD-1, ACL-7, and ADS-1 following biguanide treatment. Each of these mRNAs decreased or remain unchanged in abundance upon treatment with biguanide via quantitative RT-PCR (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G–L)
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2G–L

claim: A parallel decrease in overall levels of FARD-1::RFP protein of fard-1(oe1) transgenics was seen with phenformin treatment.
source: A parallel decrease in overall levels of FARD-1::RFP protein of fard-1(oe1) transgenics was seen with phenformin treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 2M).
evidence: Supported by fluorescence intensity data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2M

claim: The seemingly paradoxical data on ether lipid biosynthetic gene expression are likely consistent with post-translational negative feedback of ether lipids on the ether lipid biosynthetic pathway.
source: These seemingly paradoxical data are likely consistent with post-translational negative feedback of ether lipids on the ether lipid biosynthetic pathway, as has been previously reported (Honsho et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Honsho et al., 2010 and inference from the data

claim: prx-5 RNAi impairs lifespan extension prompted by phenformin fully.
source: Indeed, either prx-5 or prx-19 RNAi impair lifespan extension prompted by phenformin fully or partially, respectively (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 3A

claim: prx-19 RNAi impairs lifespan extension prompted by phenformin partially.
source: Indeed, either prx-5 or prx-19 RNAi impair lifespan extension prompted by phenformin fully or partially, respectively (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 3B

claim: PRX-5 is involved in protein import into the peroxisomal matrix.
source: PRX-5 is involved in protein import into the peroxisomal matrix and PRX-19 is involved in proper sorting of proteins for peroxisomal biogenesis.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of peroxisomal protein function

claim: PRX-19 is involved in proper sorting of proteins for peroxisomal biogenesis.
source: PRX-5 is involved in protein import into the peroxisomal matrix and PRX-19 is involved in proper sorting of proteins for peroxisomal biogenesis.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of peroxisomal protein function

claim: Either disruption of ether lipid biosynthetic machinery or of a principal site of ether lipid biosynthesis impairs phenformin's pro-longevity benefit.
source: Thus, either disruption of ether lipid biosynthetic machinery or of a principal site of ether lipid biosynthesis impairs phenformin's pro-longevity benefit.
evidence: Supported by lifespan data from ether lipid mutants and peroxisomal protein knockdowns

claim: RNAi of two fatty acid desaturases (fat-3 and fat-4) involved in the synthesis of 18- and 20-carbon PUFAs blunt phenformin-mediated lifespan extension in wild-type worms.
source: Indeed, RNAi knockdown of two fatty acid desaturases and two fatty acid elongases in phenformin-treated C. elegans blunted phenformin-stimulated lifespan extension relative to empty vector controls (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 3D–E

claim: RNAi of two fatty acid elongases (elo-1 and elo-2) involved in the synthesis of 18- and 20-carbon PUFAs blunt phenformin-mediated lifespan extension in wild-type worms.
source: Indeed, RNAi knockdown of two fatty acid desaturases and two fatty acid elongases in phenformin-treated C. elegans blunted phenformin-stimulated lifespan extension relative to empty vector controls (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 3F–G

claim: These four genes (fat-3, fat-4, elo-1, and elo-2) all contribute to the production of fatty acids 18–20 carbons in length with three or more double bonds.
source: Notably, these four genes all contribute to the production of fatty acids 18–20 carbons in length with three or more double bonds.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of fatty acid biosynthesis pathway in C. elegans

claim: RNAi knockdown of fatty acid desaturases and elongases in C. elegans results in inherent lifespan extension on vehicle relative to wild-type controls on empty vector RNAi.
source: Although knockdown of fatty acid desaturases and elongases in C. elegans results in inherent lifespan extension on vehicle relative to wild-type controls on empty vector RNAi as has been previously reported (Shmookler Reis et al., 2011; Horikawa et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to Shmookler Reis et al., 2011; Horikawa et al., 2008

claim: RNAi knockdown of fat-3, fat-4, elo-1, and elo-2 mitigate phenformin-driven lifespan extension.
source: RNAi knockdown of fat-3, fat-4, elo-1, and elo-2 mitigate phenformin-driven lifespan extension (Figure 3D–G).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 3D–G

claim: Specific fatty acid desaturases and elongases may promote biguanide-mediated lifespan extension through contribution of long and polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) to the synthesis of ether lipids.
source: These results suggest the tantalizing possibility that specific fatty acid desaturases and elongases promote biguanide-mediated lifespan extension through contribution of long and polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) to the synthesis of ether lipids, though a mechanistically distinct role is also possible.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the data with acknowledgment of alternative possibilities

claim: Knockdown of fard-1, acl-7, and ads-1 by RNAi results in suppression of lifespan extension in isp-1, raga-1, and eat-2 mutants.
source: Knockdown of fard-1, acl-7, and ads-1 by RNAi results in suppression of lifespan extension in isp-1, raga-1, and eat-2 mutants (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 4A–C

claim: Knockdown of ether lipid synthesis genes by RNAi did not impact lifespan extension in daf-2 mutants.
source: However, knockdown of ether lipid synthesis genes by RNAi did not impact lifespan extension in daf-2 mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The ether lipid biosynthetic machinery plays a broad role in lifespan extension.
source: Thus, the ether lipid biosynthetic machinery plays a broad role in lifespan extension, and, importantly, does not non-selectively shorten lifespan by making animals generally unfit.
evidence: Inferred from the selective requirement in multiple longevity paradigms but not daf-2

claim: The ether lipid biosynthetic machinery does not non-selectively shorten lifespan by making animals generally unfit.
source: Thus, the ether lipid biosynthetic machinery plays a broad role in lifespan extension, and, importantly, does not non-selectively shorten lifespan by making animals generally unfit.
evidence: Inferred from the selective requirement in some but not all longevity paradigms

claim: fard-1(oe1) alone significantly extends lifespan.
source: Strikingly, fard-1(oe1) alone significantly extends lifespan (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 5A

claim: A second, independent fard-1(oe2) transgenic line shows similar lifespan extension.
source: This result is similar in a second, independent fard-1(oe2) transgenic line (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Knockdown of three ether lipid biosynthetic enzymes leads to significant suppression of fard-1(oe1) lifespan extension.
source: As predicted, knockdown of three ether lipid biosynthetic enzymes leads to significant suppression of fard-1(oe1) lifespan extension (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B

claim: Both phenformin treatment and fard-1 overexpression in fard-1(oe) animals non-additively reduce endogenous mRNA expression of fard-1 by ~40%.
source: We observe that both phenformin treatment and fard-1 overexpression in fard-1(oe) animals non-additively reduce endogenous mRNA expression of fard-1 by ~40% (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Lifespan extension attributable to fard-1(oe1) is suppressed by knockdown of skn-1/Nrf, aak-2/AMPK, and daf-16/FoxO.
source: Lifespan extension attributable to fard-1(oe1) is suppressed by these three gene knockdowns (Figure 5E–G)
evidence: Supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 5E–G

claim: skn-1/Nrf and aak-2/AMPK have previously been demonstrated to be necessary for metformin-stimulated lifespan extension.
source: While skn-1/Nrf and aak-2/AMPK have previously been demonstrated to be necessary for metformin-stimulated lifespan extension, daf-16/FoxO has not (Onken and Driscoll, 2010; Kenyon et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to Onken and Driscoll, 2010; Kenyon et al., 1993

claim: daf-16/FoxO has not been demonstrated to be necessary for metformin-stimulated lifespan extension.
source: While skn-1/Nrf and aak-2/AMPK have previously been demonstrated to be necessary for metformin-stimulated lifespan extension, daf-16/FoxO has not (Onken and Driscoll, 2010; Kenyon et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to Onken and Driscoll, 2010; Kenyon et al., 1993

claim: fard-1(oe) promotes mechanistically distinct lifespan extension in C. elegans.
source: In aggregate, these results support the notion that ether lipids are an important requirement in multiple, diverse longevity paradigms, and further that fard-1(oe) promotes mechanistically distinct lifespan extension in C. elegans.
evidence: Inferred from the different genetic requirements for fard-1(oe) vs. biguanide-mediated lifespan extension

claim: Levels of 16:0 and 18:1 alkenyl ether lipids are significantly increased in fard-1(oe3) transgenic animals versus wild-type worms.
source: Levels of 16:0 and 18:1 alkenyl ether lipids (indicated by DMAs on GC-MS analysis) are significantly increased in fard-1(oe3) transgenic animals versus wild-type worms (Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by GC-MS data shown in Figure 5H

claim: 18:0 DMA ether lipids were not increased in fard-1(oe3) transgenic animals, indicating that the ether lipid pool has both similarities and differences between fard-1 overexpression and phenformin treatment.
source: By comparison, 18:0 DMA ether lipids were not increased, indicating that the ether lipid pool has both similarities and differences between fard-1 overexpression and phenformin treatment.
evidence: Supported by GC-MS data shown in Figure 5H and comparison to phenformin data

claim: The PUFAs 20:4 arachidonate and 20:5 eicosapentaenoate are increased in fard-1(oe3) transgenic animals.
source: Those exhibiting increases in fard-1(oe) include the PUFAs 20:4 arachidonate and 20:5 eicosapentaenoate.
evidence: Supported by GC-MS data shown in Figure 5I

claim: PUFAs may play a mechanistic role in lifespan extension in fard-1(oe) or they may be increased because of longevity-promoting activity of ether lipids.
source: This suggests either that PUFAs play a mechanistic role in lifespan extension in fard-1(oe) or that they are increased because of longevity-promoting activity of ether lipids.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the PUFA increase data

claim: gpx-1 RNAi leads to variable lifespan extension relative to wild-type controls and exhibits non-additive lifespan extension with fard-1(oe).
source: This analysis indicates that gpx-1 (ortholog of human GPX4) RNAi leads to variable lifespan extension relative to wild-type controls and exhibits non-additive lifespan extension with fard-1(oe) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C

claim: Neither gpx-6 nor gpx-7 knockdown impacts lifespan extension in fard-1(oe) animals.
source: Neither gpx-6 nor gpx-7 knockdown impacts lifespan extension in fard-1(oe) animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–E

claim: GPX family RNAi do not negatively impact lifespan extension reproducibly downstream of phenformin.
source: Further, GPX family RNAi do not negatively impact lifespan extension reproducibly downstream of phenformin (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F–H).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F–H

claim: It is unlikely that phenformin-prompted or fard-1(oe) lifespan extension occurs by suppressing ferroptosis.
source: We conclude that genetic triggers that induce ferroptosis do not impact phenformin-prompted or fard-1(oe) lifespan extension, and thus it is unlikely that either extend lifespan by suppressing ferroptosis.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effect of GPX knockdowns on lifespan extension

claim: Intestinal lipid droplets are significantly less numerous following phenformin treatment.
source: Indeed, quantitative analysis indicates that intestinal lipid droplets are significantly less numerous following phenformin treatment (in glo-4 RNAi-treated FARD-1::RFP transgenics (fard-1 oe3) fed C1-BODIPY-C12 to label lipid droplets, Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by lipid droplet quantification data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Gain-of-function mutations in skn-1/Nrf prompt age-dependent, somatic depletion of fat (Asdf).
source: We previously reported that gain-of-function mutations in the nutrient- and stress-responsive transcription factor skn-1/Nrf prompt age-dependent, somatic depletion of fat (Asdf) (Lynn et al., 2015; Nhan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lynn et al., 2015; Nhan et al., 2019

claim: Phenformin treatment produces Asdf at day 3 of adulthood, a phenotype that is quantitatively analogous to and non-additive with skn-1 gain-of-function mutants.
source: Strikingly, we found that phenformin treatment produces Asdf at day 3 of adulthood, a phenotype that is quantitatively analogous to and non-additive with skn-1 gain-of-function mutants (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: Supported by Oil-red-O staining data shown in Figure 6B–C

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in any of the three ether lipid biosynthetic genes completely prevent the phenformin-mediated Asdf phenotype.
source: Compellingly, loss-of-function mutations in any of the three ether lipid biosynthetic genes completely prevent the phenformin-mediated Asdf phenotype (Figure 6B–C)
evidence: Supported by Oil-red-O staining data shown in Figure 6B–C

claim: Ether lipids mechanistically connect phenformin to promotion of skn-1-dependent pro-longevity metabolic defenses.
source: suggesting that ether lipids mechanistically connect phenformin to promotion of skn-1-dependent pro-longevity metabolic defenses.
evidence: Inferred from the requirement of ether lipids for phenformin-mediated Asdf

claim: fard-1 overexpressing animals display an intermediate Asdf phenotype, with moderate enhancement by phenformin treatment.
source: As expected, fard-1 overexpressing animals also display an intermediate Asdf phenotype, with moderate enhancement by phenformin treatment (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: Supported by Oil-red-O staining data shown in Figure 6B–C

claim: Biguanide-mediated lipid shifts are abrogated in skn-1 loss-of-function mutant animals.
source: Finally, the Asdf lipid shift evident with phenformin treatment requires skn-1, as biguanide-mediated lipid shifts are abrogated in skn-1 loss-of-function mutant animals (Figure 6D–E).
evidence: Supported by Oil-red-O staining data shown in Figure 6D–E

claim: Ether lipids connect biguanides to activation of metabolic stress defenses and longevity downstream of SKN-1.
source: In aggregate, these data indicate that ether lipids connect biguanides to activation of metabolic stress defenses and longevity downstream of SKN-1.
evidence: Inferred from the requirement of ether lipids and skn-1 for phenformin-mediated Asdf and lifespan extension

claim: SKN-1 activates a metabolic stress defense response to drive somatic lipid depletion through enhancing lipid utilization and innate immunity gene expression that opposes canonical oxidative stress responses.
source: Our previous work determined that SKN-1 activates a metabolic stress defense response to drive somatic lipid depletion through enhancing lipid utilization and innate immunity gene expression that opposes canonical oxidative stress responses (Nhan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nhan et al., 2019

claim: Phenformin treatment reduces expression of the canonical oxidative stress response gene gst-4 irrespective of bacterial diet source.
source: Concordant with the hypothesis that biguanides activate SKN-1 metabolic/innate immune and not oxidative stress defenses, phenformin treatment reduces expression of the canonical oxidative stress response gene gst-4 irrespective of bacterial diet source (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B)
evidence: Supported by GFP reporter data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B

claim: Phenformin induces expression of the innate immune response gene dod-24 in a manner dependent both upon skn-1 and ether lipids.
source: while reciprocally inducing expression of the innate immune response gene dod-24 in a manner dependent both upon skn-1 and ether lipids (Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by GFP reporter data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C

claim: Biguanides activate an ether lipid-skn-1 signaling relay to drive longevity.
source: Together with the observation that promotion of lifespan extension by both phenformin and fard-1(oe) require skn-1, these data suggest that biguanides activate an ether lipid-skn-1 signaling relay to drive longevity.
evidence: Inferred from the requirement of ether lipids and skn-1 for biguanide and fard-1(oe) lifespan extension

claim: Biguanide treatment significantly reduces somatic total fatty acid levels in wild-type adult day 1 nematodes.
source: Analysis of wild-type adult day 1 nematodes treated with phenformin on live OP50-1 indicates that biguanide treatment significantly reduces somatic total fatty acid levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B–C)
evidence: Supported by GC-MS data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B–C

claim: Biguanides can significantly reduce somatic fatty acid levels irrespective of whether the bacterial food source is live vs. dead and metabolically inactive.
source: This result was preserved in wild-type animals grown on metabolically inactive PFA-treated OP50-1 as a food source, indicating that biguanides can significantly reduce somatic fatty acid levels irrespective of whether the bacterial food source is live vs. dead and metabolically inactive (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: Supported by GC-MS data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B–C

claim: Despite significant reduction of overall fatty acids, biguanides preferentially protect levels of ether lipid-derived 16:0 DMA and 18:1 DMA, irrespective of bacterial growth status.
source: Notably, despite this significant reduction of overall fatty acids, biguanides preferentially protect levels of ether lipid-derived 16:0 DMA and 18:1 DMA, again irrespective of bacterial growth status (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D–E).
evidence: Supported by GC-MS data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D–E

claim: Biguanides lead to relative increases in ether lipid levels through direct action in the nematode, rather than through indirect effects in the bacterial food source.
source: Thus, we conclude that biguanides lead to relative increases in ether lipid levels through direct action in the nematode, rather than through indirect effects in the bacterial food source.
evidence: Inferred from the preservation of ether lipid effects with metabolically inactive bacteria

claim: Metformin and phenformin both extend lifespan in wild-type animals whether grown on live or PFA-treated E. coli OP50-1.
source: First, and in contrast to prior studies suggesting that lifespan requires drug effects on the Escherichia coli (Cabreiro et al., 2013; Pryor et al., 2019), we noted that under experimental conditions tested, metformin and phenformin both extend lifespan in wild-type animals whether grown on live or PFA-treated E. coli OP50-1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A–F).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A–F

claim: ads-1 deficiency completely blunts both metformin and phenformin-mediated lifespan extension irrespective of bacterial food source growth conditions.
source: Consistent with the effect of biguanides on both lifespan and ether lipids being via direct action on the nematode, ads-1 deficiency completely blunts both metformin and phenformin-mediated lifespan extension irrespective of bacterial food source growth conditions (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A–F).
evidence: Supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A–F

claim: Biguanides increase proportions of ether lipids and require activated ether lipid machinery to exert pro-longevity benefits through direct drug action on the nematode.
source: In aggregate, these data suggest that biguanides increase proportions of ether lipids and require activated ether lipid machinery to exert pro-longevity benefits through direct drug action on the nematode.
evidence: Inferred from the preservation of ether lipid and lifespan effects with metabolically inactive bacteria

claim: Differences in ether lipid abundance and composition are correlated with diseases of aging.
source: Differences in ether lipid abundance and composition are correlated with diseases of aging.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from the literature

claim: The uniform lethality associated with human genetic ether lipid deficiency has made it difficult to study the role of ether lipids in aging and aging-associated diseases.
source: The uniform lethality associated with human genetic ether lipid deficiency, as in the case of patients diagnosed with RCDP and Zellweger syndrome, has made it difficult to study the role of ether lipids in aging and aging-associated diseases (Braverman et al., 1997; Motley et al., 1997; Purdue et al., 1997; Itzkovitz et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Braverman et al., 1997; Motley et al., 1997; Purdue et al., 1997; Itzkovitz et al., 2012

claim: Observational studies demonstrate decreases in certain plasmalogen species in Alzheimer's disease.
source: Nonetheless, observational studies demonstrate decreases in certain plasmalogen species in Alzheimer's disease, suggesting a probable link between ether lipids and aging-related pathologies (Grimm et al., 2011; Goodenowe et al., 2007; Han et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Grimm et al., 2011; Goodenowe et al., 2007; Han et al., 2001

claim: Loss of the ether lipid biosynthetic machinery benefits cancer cell survival by enhancing resistance to ferroptosis.
source: Ether lipids have conflicting roles in cancer; while loss of the ether lipid biosynthetic machinery profits cancer cell survival by enhancing resistance to ferroptosis (Zou et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to Zou et al., 2020

claim: In some contexts, ether lipid deficiency results in impaired pathogenicity in various human cancer cells.
source: in other contexts, ether lipid deficiency results in impaired pathogenicity in various human cancer cells (Benjamin et al., 2013; Perez et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Benjamin et al., 2013; Perez et al., 2020

claim: Cancer cells generally have higher levels of ether lipids compared to normal cells.
source: Cancer cells generally have higher levels of ether lipids compared to normal cells, leading others to suggest that ether lipids confer pro-survival benefit (Benjamin et al., 2013; Albert and Anderson, 1977; Snyder and Wood, 1969).
evidence: Supported by citations to Benjamin et al., 2013; Albert and Anderson, 1977; Snyder and Wood, 1969

claim: Certain ether lipid species have been reported to have anti-tumor properties.
source: However, certain ether lipid species have also been reported to have anti-tumor properties (Jaffrès et al., 2016; Arthur and Bittman, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jaffrès et al., 2016; Arthur and Bittman, 2014

claim: There is an association between ether lipid content and animal longevity in long-lived animal models such as the naked mole-rat and the mud clam Arctica islandica.
source: Studies in long-lived animal models suggest that there is an association between ether lipid content and animal longevity, such as in the naked mole-rat (Heterocephalus glaber) (Mitchell et al., 2007) and the mud clam Arctica islandica (Munro and Blier, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mitchell et al., 2007 and Munro and Blier, 2012

claim: Higher plasmalogen levels in naked mole-rat tissues versus mice are speculated to contribute to protection of cellular membranes via a reduction of oxidative stress.
source: Higher plasmalogen levels in naked mole-rat tissues versus mice are speculated to contribute to protection of cellular membranes via a reduction of oxidative stress (Mitchell et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mitchell et al., 2007 and speculative language

claim: Exceptionally long-lived humans harbor higher levels of phosphatidylcholine-derived, short chained alkyl ether lipids and lower levels of phosphatidylethanolamine-derived longer chained plasmalogens.
source: Similarly, exceptionally long-lived humans harbor higher levels of phosphatidylcholine-derived, short chained alkyl ether lipids and a lower levels of phosphatidylethanolamine-derived longer chained plasmalogens (Pradas et al., 2019), but these associations are of unclear functional significance.
evidence: Supported by citation to Pradas et al., 2019

claim: Ether lipid deficiency in C. elegans prevents longevity downstream of mitochondrial electron transport chain dysfunction, mTOR deficiency, caloric restriction, and biguanides.
source: Although it is clear from work presented here that ether lipid deficiency in C. elegans prevents longevity downstream of mitochondrial electron transport chain dysfunction, mTOR deficiency, caloric restriction, and biguanides alike
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Each longevity paradigm (mitochondrial dysfunction, mTOR deficiency, caloric restriction, biguanides) has features of nutrient deficiency, energy stress, or nutrient sensing.
source: Each of these longevity paradigms has features of nutrient deficiency, energy stress, or nutrient sensing, so it is possible that ether lipids are at least part of the common effector arm conferring benefit in aging to various forms of metabolic stress.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of these longevity paradigms and speculation

claim: daf-2 loss-of-function does not require ether lipid biosynthetic machinery and yet has a clear requirement for skn-1.
source: It is particularly interesting that daf-2 loss-of-function does not require ether lipid biosynthetic machinery and yet has a clear requirement for skn-1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: It is possible to activate skn-1 through multiple, parallel mechanisms, only some of which require ether lipids.
source: These observations suggest the very likely possibilities that (1) it is possible to activate skn-1 through multiple, parallel mechanisms, only some of which require ether lipids
evidence: Inferred from the differential requirement of ether lipids in different longevity paradigms that require skn-1

claim: There are multiple modes of skn-1 activation that promote longevity, each of which has distinct transcriptional programs.
source: and (2) that there are multiple modes of skn-1 activation that promote longevity, each of which has distinct transcriptional programs (Nhan et al., 2019; Castillo-Quan et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nhan et al., 2019; Castillo-Quan et al., 2023 and inference from data

claim: Unsaturated fatty acids and phosphatidylethanolamine ether lipids are essential to the health-promoting effects of biguanides.
source: Our results suggest that unsaturated fatty acids and phosphatidylethanolamine ether lipids are essential to the health-promoting effects of biguanides.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data on ether lipids and fatty acid desaturases/elongases

claim: Disruption of ether lipid biosynthesis has been shown to increase the proportion of stearate (18:0) and other saturated fatty acids.
source: Additionally, disruption of ether lipid biosynthesis has been shown to increase the proportion of stearate (18:0) and other saturated fatty acids (Shi et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shi et al., 2016

claim: Ether lipid synthesis is likely to be regulated post-translationally by biguanide treatment.
source: Based upon our findings, ether lipid synthesis is likely to be regulated post-translationally by biguanide treatment.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that mRNA levels decrease while ether lipid levels increase

claim: The demonstrated increases in plasmalogens and specific ether lipids are consistent with increases in activity of the ether lipid biosynthetic machinery.
source: The demonstrated increases in plasmalogens and specific ether lipids are both consistent with increases in activity of the ether lipid biosynthetic machinery.
evidence: Inferred from the metabolomic data

claim: The decreases in mRNAs for acl-7, ads-1, and fard-1 prompted by phenformin treatment and by overexpression of fard-1 invoke negative feedback of the end product(s) of ether lipid biogenesis on transcription of genes encoding ether lipid biosynthetic enzymes.
source: While we do not understand the mechanism for the increased activity of ether lipid synthesizing enzymes, the decreases in mRNAs for acl-7, ads-1, and fard-1 prompted by phenformin treatment and by overexpression of fard-1 alike invoke negative feedback of the end product(s) of ether lipid biogenesis on transcription of genes encoding ether lipid biosynthetic enzymes.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of decreased mRNA with increased ether lipids

claim: Higher levels of ether lipids promote proteasomal degradation of peroxisomal Far1 protein.
source: It should be noted that this possibility is consistent with previous work showing that higher levels of ether lipids promote proteasomal degradation of peroxisomal Far1 protein (Honsho et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Honsho et al., 2010

claim: Ether lipids are required for phenformin to activate metabolic defenses downstream of the stress- and metabolism-responsive transcription factor skn-1/Nrf.
source: Strikingly, our data demonstrate for the first time that ether lipids are required for phenformin to activate metabolic defenses downstream of the stress- and metabolism-responsive transcription factor skn-1/Nrf.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Biguanides do not stimulate canonical skn-1 antioxidant defenses such as gst-4 expression.
source: Based upon our own work, biguanides do not stimulate canonical skn-1 antioxidant defenses such as gst-4 expression, in contrast to the subtle effects seen in the existing literature (Cabreiro et al., 2013; Onken and Driscoll, 2010).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to Cabreiro et al., 2013; Onken and Driscoll, 2010

claim: skn-1 is uniquely required for metabolic stress defenses downstream of metformin such as Asdf, rather than canonical oxidative or proteostatic defenses.
source: We suggest that skn-1 is uniquely required for metabolic stress defenses downstream of metformin such as Asdf, rather than canonical oxidative or proteostatic defenses.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data on gst-4 and dod-24 expression

claim: The requirement for ether lipids in Asdf activation by phenformin confirms that this class of lipids plays a heretofore unappreciated role in a distinct form of skn-1 activation.
source: Thus, the requirement for ether lipids in Asdf activation by phenformin confirm that this class of lipids plays a heretofore unappreciated role in a distinct form of skn-1 activation mimicked by genetic forms of skn-1 activation that we have previously reported (Lynn et al., 2015; Nhan et al., 2019).
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data and citations to Lynn et al., 2015; Nhan et al., 2019

claim: Lifespan extension resulting from overexpression of fard-1 shows mechanistic similarities and dissimilarities from biguanide action in longevity.
source: Lifespan extension resulting from overexpression of fard-1 shows mechanistic similarities and dissimilarities from biguanide action in longevity.
evidence: Inferred from the different genetic requirements for fard-1(oe) vs. biguanide-mediated lifespan extension

claim: fard-1 overexpression requires intact skn-1 and AMPK action.
source: Curiously, and concordant with the idea that ether lipids participate in the activation of skn-1, fard-1 overexpression requires intact skn-1 and AMPK action.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Biguanides do not require daf-16/FoxO, but fard-1 overexpression does.
source: Discordantly, biguanides do not require daf-16/FoxO, but fard-1 overexpression does.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: fard-1 overexpression may alter the ether lipid landscape in a manner not analogous to biguanide treatment, either in distinct tissues or with regard to different ether lipid molecular species.
source: It could be that fard-1 overexpression alters the ether lipid landscape in a manner not analogous to biguanide treatment, either in distinct tissues or with regard to different ether lipid molecular species, and that these differences have distinct molecular effectors.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the differences between fard-1(oe) and biguanide effects

claim: The degree of ether lipid alteration may be different following biguanide treatment vs. fard-1 overexpression.
source: Second, the degree of ether lipid alteration may be different following biguanide treatment vs. fard-1 overexpression.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the differences between fard-1(oe) and biguanide effects

claim: It is highly likely that distinct effector mechanisms are required by biguanides versus fard-1 overexpression based upon the myriad potential direct and indirect sites of action of biguanides in aging.
source: Finally, it is highly likely based upon the myriad potential direct and indirect sites of action of biguanides in aging, including but not limited to mitochondria, lysosomes, the nuclear pore complex, mTOR, and AMPK that distinct effector mechanisms are required by biguanides versus fard-1 overexpression (Cabreiro et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2017; Pryor et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2022; Wheaton et al., 2014; Onken and Driscoll, 2010; Espada et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on biguanide mechanisms and speculation

claim: Ether lipid biosynthesis plays a broader role in aging than previously described.
source: In aggregate, data presented here indicate that ether lipid biosynthesis plays a broader role in aging than previously described.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing requirement in multiple longevity paradigms

claim: The necessity of the ether lipid machinery in metformin- and phenformin-stimulated lifespan extension and in multiple longevity paradigms indicates that ether lipids serve as a lynchpin through which lifespan is modulated.
source: The necessity of the ether lipid machinery in metformin- and phenformin-stimulated lifespan extension and in multiple longevity paradigms indicates that ether lipids serve as a lynchpin through which lifespan is modulated (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data and illustrated in Figure 7A–B

claim: Overexpression of fard-1 alone results in lifespan extension, providing an opportunity to identify ether lipids that promote health and the effector mechanisms through which they act.
source: Our demonstration that overexpression of fard-1 alone results in lifespan extension provides an exciting opportunity to identify ether lipids that promote health and the effector mechanisms through which they act.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and speculation about future research directions

claim: Modulation of ether lipids pharmacologically or dietarily may provide a new potential therapeutic target in aging and aging-related diseases.
source: Finally, these results support the exciting possibility that modulation of ether lipids pharmacologically or even dietarily may provide a new potential therapeutic target in aging and aging-related diseases.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the implications of the findings
